objectives: Compare dietary assessment methods: 24-hour recall, food-frequency questionnaires, and food diaries, with their strengths and biases.
Interpret the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, MyPlate (versus the older Food Guide Pyramid), and evidence-based dietary patterns (Mediterranean, DASH).
Apply glycemic index and load and read a Nutrition Facts label correctly.

slides.title: Measuring what people eat: assessment methods
slides.body:
Before a nutritionist can advise a client or a researcher can study a population, they must first **measure dietary intake** — a notoriously difficult task, because eating is frequent, varied, and easily misreported. Several established **dietary assessment methods** each balance accuracy, burden, and time frame.

The **24-hour dietary recall** asks a person to report everything eaten and drunk in the previous day, usually in a structured interview. Its strengths are low respondent burden and that it does not alter eating behavior (the food has already been eaten). Its weaknesses are reliance on memory and the fact that a single day is unrepresentative of usual intake. To address this, large surveys use **multiple non-consecutive recalls** and statistical methods such as the **Automated Self-Administered 24-Hour (ASA24)** tool and the **USDA Automated Multiple-Pass Method (AMPM)**. The U.S. national survey **NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey)**, run by the **CDC**, uses 24-hour recalls to monitor the nation's diet.

The **food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ)** asks how often, on average, a person consumes each of a long list of foods over a longer period (months to a year). Its strength is capturing **usual, long-term intake** cheaply in large studies; its weakness is reduced precision and reliance on the fixed food list and on memory. The most influential FFQ was developed by **Walter Willett** at the **Harvard School of Public Health** and used in landmark cohorts such as the **Nurses' Health Study** and the **Health Professionals Follow-up Study**.

The **food diary (food record)** asks a person to write down (or photograph) foods at the time of eating, ideally weighing portions. It is the most accurate of the self-report methods because it does not depend on memory, but it carries the highest burden and can itself **change eating behavior** (the act of recording makes people eat differently or less).

All self-report methods share a fundamental problem: **misreporting**, especially **underreporting of energy intake**, which is more common among people with obesity. To detect it, researchers use **biomarkers** and reference methods — most famously the **doubly labeled water (DLW)** technique, which measures total energy expenditure (and hence, at weight stability, intake) by tracking the disappearance of two stable isotopes ($^2\text{H}$ and $^{18}\text{O}$) from the body. DLW studies repeatedly show that self-reported intake underestimates true intake by 10–30%. A skilled nutritionist therefore treats any single assessment as an estimate and triangulates across methods and time.

slides.title: From the Food Guide Pyramid to MyPlate and the Dietary Guidelines
slides.body:
Governments translate nutrition science into public guidance. In the United States, the foundational document is the **Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA)**, jointly issued by the **U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)** and the **Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)** and updated every five years, the first edition appearing in **1980** and the current edition being **2020–2025**. The DGA distills the evidence into practical advice: emphasize vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat dairy; limit added sugars (to under 10% of calories), saturated fat (under 10%), and sodium (under 2300 mg/day); and follow a healthy eating pattern across the lifespan.

To communicate these principles visually, the USDA has used food-group icons. The famous **Food Guide Pyramid**, introduced in **1992**, placed grains at the wide base (6–11 servings) and fats at the narrow tip. It was criticized for over-emphasizing refined grains and for being hard to apply at the plate. In **2005** it was restyled as **MyPyramid**, and in **2011** it was replaced entirely by **MyPlate** under the leadership of First Lady **Michelle Obama**. MyPlate depicts a place setting divided into four sections — **fruits, vegetables, grains, and protein** — with a side circle for **dairy**. Its core message is simple and portion-oriented: **fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables**, make at least half your grains whole, and vary your protein sources. The shift from pyramid to plate reflects a move from abstract serving counts toward an intuitive, meal-based model.

Alongside official guidance, nutrition science has identified **dietary patterns** with strong evidence for health, two of which dominate practice:

- The **Mediterranean diet**, based on the traditional eating habits of countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea, emphasizes olive oil, vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, whole grains, fish, and moderate wine, with little red meat. Its cardiovascular benefits were popularized by **Ancel Keys** through the **Seven Countries Study** and confirmed by the Spanish randomized trial **PREDIMED (2013)**, which found significant reductions in cardiovascular events.
- The **DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension)**, developed through **NIH**-funded trials published in **1997**, emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while restricting sodium, saturated fat, and sweets. It reliably lowers blood pressure and is repeatedly ranked among the best overall diets by **U.S. News & World Report**.

These evidence-based patterns give nutritionists concrete, well-studied frameworks to recommend, grounded in the same science the DGA summarizes.

slides.title: Glycemic load and reading the Nutrition Facts label
slides.body:
Translating guidelines into food choices requires two practical skills: gauging a food's blood-sugar impact and reading the **Nutrition Facts label**.

As introduced earlier, the **glycemic index (GI)** ranks a carbohydrate food by its blood-glucose-raising effect relative to pure glucose (=100). But GI describes a fixed test dose and ignores how much carbohydrate is actually in a serving. The **glycemic load (GL)** corrects this by combining quality and quantity:

$$\text{GL} = \frac{\text{GI} \times \text{available carbohydrate (g) per serving}}{100}$$

A watermelon, for example, has a high GI (~72) but little carbohydrate per serving, so its glycemic load is low. Conversely, a large serving of even a moderate-GI food can carry a high glycemic load. By convention, a GL **≤ 10 is low**, **11–19 is medium**, and **≥ 20 is high** per serving. Glycemic load is the more meaningful predictor of a meal's real glucose response and is useful in counseling clients with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The **Nutrition Facts label**, mandated in the U.S. by the **Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990** and overseen by the **FDA**, is the consumer's primary tool. Its 2016 redesign (mandatory compliance from 2020) emphasizes the most decision-relevant numbers. To read it correctly, a nutritionist teaches clients to check, in order:

- **Serving size** — every other number on the label refers to *one serving*, and packages often contain several servings. A common error is reading the calories for the whole package as if it were one serving.
- **Calories per serving** — the energy in one serving.
- **% Daily Value (%DV)** — how much one serving contributes to a 2000-kcal reference diet. A useful rule of thumb: **5% DV or less is low; 20% DV or more is high** for that nutrient.
- **Nutrients to limit** — saturated fat, sodium, and the now separately listed **added sugars** (distinguished from naturally occurring sugars since the 2016 redesign).
- **Nutrients to get enough of** — dietary fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium (the four micronutrients of public-health concern listed since 2016).

Ingredients are listed by **descending weight**, so the first few ingredients dominate the product. Reading the label together with the glycemic-load concept lets a client see, for instance, that a 'low-fat' snack may still carry a high added-sugar content and a high glycemic load. These two skills — interpreting glycemic load and reading the label critically, including the all-important serving size — turn the abstract Dietary Guidelines into everyday decisions at the grocery store.

question.question: A researcher wants to estimate the usual long-term intake of thousands of participants in a large cohort study as cheaply as possible. Which dietary assessment method is best suited, and what is its main limitation?
options: A weighed food diary, because it is cheap and changes behavior to give the truest picture.
A food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ), because it captures usual long-term intake inexpensively at scale; its main limitation is reduced precision and reliance on memory and a fixed food list.
A single 24-hour recall, because one day perfectly represents a person's habitual diet.
Doubly labeled water, because it directly records every food eaten.
question.explanation: For large cohorts needing usual long-term intake at low cost, the FFQ (e.g., Willett's Harvard FFQ used in the Nurses' Health Study) is the standard choice; its limitation is lower precision and dependence on memory and the fixed food list. A weighed diary is accurate but high-burden and can change behavior; a single 24-hour recall captures only one (unrepresentative) day; and doubly labeled water measures total energy expenditure, not the content of foods eaten.

hints: Which method asks about average frequency over months and scales to thousands of people?
Think about the Nurses' Health Study and Walter Willett.
slides.workedSolution: The FFQ captures habitual long-term intake cheaply across large populations; its weakness is precision and memory/list dependence. Diaries are accurate but burdensome; single recalls capture only one day; doubly labeled water measures expenditure, not food content.

question.question: Which statement best describes the shift from the 1992 Food Guide Pyramid to the 2011 MyPlate icon?
options: MyPlate increased the recommended servings of refined grains compared with the pyramid.

MyPlate replaced the pyramid's abstract serving counts with an intuitive plate divided into fruits, vegetables, grains, and protein (plus a dairy side), with the message to fill half the plate with fruits and vegetables.
MyPlate eliminated all guidance about vegetables and fruits.
MyPlate was introduced in 1980 as the first-ever federal dietary icon.
question.explanation: MyPlate (2011, championed by Michelle Obama) replaced the Food Guide Pyramid (1992) and its MyPyramid restyle (2005). It uses a place-setting divided into fruits, vegetables, grains, and protein with a dairy side, conveying the practical message to fill half the plate with produce and make at least half of grains whole. The pyramid had been criticized for over-emphasizing grains; MyPlate did not increase refined grains, did not remove produce guidance, and was not the 1980 first edition (that was the text Dietary Guidelines).

hints: The pyramid used serving counts; MyPlate uses a literal plate.
The headline rule is 'half your plate, fruits and vegetables.'
slides.workedSolution: MyPlate (2011) replaced the pyramid with an intuitive plate (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein + dairy), emphasizing filling half the plate with produce and making half of grains whole. It reduced, not increased, the emphasis on grains relative to the criticized 1992 pyramid.

A cereal box lists a serving size of 40 g at 150 kcal per serving. A client actually pours and eats 120 g in one bowl. How many kilocalories did the client consume? (Compute servings eaten × calories per serving.)
Decoding a 'healthy' snack label with a client
question.prompt: A client brings you a granola bar marketed as 'all-natural and low-fat' and says she eats two bars as an afternoon snack. The Nutrition Facts label shows a serving size of one bar (the package contains two bars), 190 kcal per serving, 16 g of total sugars including 12 g added sugars, and 2 g of fiber; the first three ingredients are brown rice syrup, oats, and cane sugar. Using your knowledge of serving size, %DV, added versus total sugars, glycemic load, and ingredient ordering, explain to her how to read this label critically. Address why 'low-fat' does not mean low-calorie or low-sugar, how the serving-size detail changes her true intake, and what the ingredient list reveals about the product.
